To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the D2 line can be used for cooling of 87Rb; (b) this cooling is based on a “quasi-dark states” mechanism, and (c) the phase-space density is increased by a factor of about 8 with respect to ordinary cooling on the D1 line.

“Laser cooling based on dark-states, i.e. decoupled states, is effective on the D2, instead of the D1, transition of 87Rb atoms, and leads to temperatures as low as 4 μK, and an increase of an order of magnitude with respect to ordinary sub-Doppler laser cooling.”

the cooling of 87Rb on the D2 optical transition is possible, and that this cooling is more efficient than on the D1 optical transition, as it provides a higher phase-space density and a lower temperature.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study and the development of novel techniques for laser cooling and trapping of neutral atoms.
the development of novel techniques to increase the phase space density in magneto-optic traps (MOT) for cold atoms and molecules.
the study of the D2 transition in the grey molasses cooling scheme for 87Rblasers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in the case of 87Rb atoms, the use of the D2 transition is not strictly mandatory for dark-state cooling and that quasi-dark states cooling can be efficiently implemented on the D2 optical transition.
the D1 transition is more suitable for laser cooling of 87Rb atoms in MOTs.

the D2 transition can be exploited to obtain a cooling rate that is comparable to that obtained on the D1 line, with the advantage that the D2 line is more efficient than the D1 line in the optical pumping process, and that the D2 light can be obtained at lower power than the D1 light.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of a quasi-dark states cooling technique can increase the number of atoms in a MOT by a factor 10, while the temperature is reduced by a factor 5.
we have demonstrated the first laser cooling of atoms in the D2 line using quasi-dark states.
, by using the Λ-enhanced grey mollasses cooling technique, the phase-space density for 87Rbbecomes comparable to the one of 87Rbcooled by the standard MOT technique.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for 85Rb and 87Rb atoms, dark-state laser cooling on the D1 line is not the only way to increase the phase space density of trapped atoms.
dark-state cooling is possible also for closed atomic transitions, provided that the atomic structure is sufficiently complicated to allow the creation of “quasi-dark states”.
dark-state laser cooling on the D2-line can be a powerful tool in the field of ultracold atoms.
